kartellrecht-grundlagen-01.question: What three categories of conduct does the cartel prohibition under Sec. 1 GWB cover?

options.a: Only written contracts between competitors
options.b: Agreements, decisions by associations of undertakings, and concerted practices
options.c: Only price-fixing in retail trade
options.d: Only conduct by dominant undertakings

kartellrecht-grundlagen-01.explanation: Sec. 1 GWB prohibits agreements between undertakings, decisions by associations of undertakings, and concerted practices that have the object or effect of preventing, restricting, or distorting competition - almost identical wording to Art. 101(1) TFEU. Important: the mere object (not only an actual effect) is sufficient.

kartellrecht-grundlagen-02.question: What does the "object or effect" wording in Sec. 1 GWB mean for so-called hardcore restrictions (e.g. price-fixing)?

options.a: Actual economic harm must always be proven
options.b: The agreement is only prohibited if both parties acted with intent
options.c: The anticompetitive object alone suffices - for hardcore restrictions, no market analysis of actual effect is required
options.d: A 10% market-share de minimis threshold applies below which no review takes place

kartellrecht-grundlagen-02.explanation: Hardcore restrictions such as price-fixing, market/customer allocation, or bid-rigging are treated as "by object" restrictions of competition: a market-analysis defense ("there was no actual effect") is not available here - the anticompetitive object alone establishes the violation.

kartellrecht-grundlagen-03.question: Under Sec. 18(4) GWB, at what market share does the rebuttable presumption of single-firm dominance apply?

options.a: From 25 percent
options.b: From 40 percent
options.c: From 60 percent
options.d: Only from 75 percent

kartellrecht-grundlagen-03.explanation: Sec. 18(4) GWB presumes an undertaking to be dominant if it holds a market share of at least 40 percent - a rebuttable presumption, not an automatic violation. Sec. 18(5)-(6) additionally sets presumption thresholds for collective dominance (e.g. up to 3 undertakings with a combined 50% share, or up to 5 undertakings with a combined two-thirds share).

kartellrecht-grundlagen-04.question: A sales director informally discusses future price-increase plans with a competitor at an industry event, with no explicit agreement reached. Is this legally unproblematic?

options.a: Yes, without a written agreement there is never a cartel violation
options.b: No - exchanging future pricing intentions can itself constitute a prohibited "concerted practice" under Sec. 1 GWB, even without an explicit agreement
options.c: Yes, as long as no specific figures are mentioned
options.d: No, this is only relevant if more than three undertakings are involved

kartellrecht-grundlagen-04.explanation: Sec. 1 GWB expressly covers "concerted practices" - an explicit agreement is not required. Exchanging information about future (not merely past) pricing intentions with a competitor, even informally at an industry event, can itself constitute the prohibited coordination. This is precisely why trade-association meetings are treated as a classic cartel-risk scenario.

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-01.question: Which of the following is NOT considered a classic hardcore restriction under competition law?

options.a: Price-fixing between competitors
options.b: Allocating customers or territories between competitors
options.c: An undertaking's unilateral internal decision to lower its own prices
options.d: Coordinated bids in public tenders (bid-rigging)

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-01.explanation: A unilateral internal pricing decision by one undertaking is simply normal competitive conduct, not an agreement or concerted practice between multiple undertakings - it lacks the necessary two-undertaking element of Sec. 1 GWB. Price-fixing, market/customer allocation, and bid-rigging, by contrast, are all recognized hardcore restrictions.

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-02.question: In June 2025 the EU Commission fined Delivery Hero and Glovo EUR 329 million. What was this case about?

options.a: Excessive delivery prices charged to end customers
options.b: A cartel agreement not to poach each other's employees ("no-poach") and to allocate markets between the two companies
options.c: Data-protection violations related to food delivery
options.d: An unlawful merger that was never notified to the Commission

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-02.explanation: This was the EU Commission's first-ever decision on a pure labour-market cartel under Art. 101 TFEU: Delivery Hero and Glovo agreed not to poach each other's employees and additionally allocated national markets between themselves - even though Delivery Hero held only a minority stake in Glovo (i.e. not full merger-control-level control). No-poach agreements between competitors are therefore a confirmed, actively enforced cartel risk, not a theoretical edge case.

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-03.question: In April 2025 the EU Commission fined 15 car manufacturers plus the industry association ACEA EUR 458 million. What made this cartel unusual?

options.a: It was a classic price-fixing agreement on new-car prices
options.b: For over 15 years, the manufacturers agreed not to advertise their vehicles' recyclability and not to compete on end-of-life-vehicle recycling payments - a cartel over non-competition on environmental information rather than price
options.c: It concerned an unlawful joint research cooperation on electric vehicles
options.d: The manufacturers agreed on common minimum warranty periods

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-03.explanation: This case shows cartels are not always about price: the manufacturers (VW receiving the largest individual amount, Mercedes-Benz obtaining full leniency immunity) agreed among themselves, for more than 15 years, not to advertise their vehicles' recyclability to customers and not to compete on end-of-life-vehicle recycling payments - an example of an information-suppression cartel under Art. 101 TFEU.

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-04.question: Why are trade-association meetings considered a classic cartel-risk scenario?

options.a: Because trade associations are fundamentally prohibited under German law
options.b: Because they can involve informal exchanges of competitively sensitive information (e.g. future pricing intentions) between competitors, which can itself constitute a concerted practice
options.c: Because mere attendance at a trade-association meeting is automatically a cartel violation
options.d: Because trade-association meetings are only permitted for state-owned undertakings

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-04.explanation: The Bundeskartellamt publishes its own guidance on competition-law-compliant trade-association work precisely because this scenario is real: competitors regularly sit together at association meetings, and informal exchanges about future prices, capacity, or terms can - even without a formal resolution - constitute a prohibited concerted practice. Mere attendance is not itself a violation; what matters is the substance of what is exchanged.

kartellrecht-bussgelder-01.question: What is the statutory fine cap under Sec. 81c(2) GWB for serious competition-law violations?

options.a: EUR 1 million per violation, regardless of the undertaking's turnover
options.b: 10 percent of the worldwide total turnover of the entire corporate group in the preceding business year
options.c: 5 percent of the affected group's domestic German turnover
options.d: There is no statutory cap - the Bundeskartellamt decides freely

kartellrecht-bussgelder-01.explanation: Sec. 81c(2) GWB caps the fine at 10 percent of the total turnover achieved by the undertaking or association of undertakings in the preceding business year. Per Abs. 5, this means the worldwide turnover of the entire economic unit (corporate group), not just the individual participating legal entity. For less serious violations, Abs. 3 sets a lower 1% cap.

kartellrecht-bussgelder-02.question: What role does an effective compliance program play in fine assessment under Sec. 81d GWB?

options.a: A compliance program has no legal relevance whatsoever to the fine amount
options.b: Appropriate and effective precautions to prevent and detect violations - taken both before and after the offense - can be considered as a mitigating factor when assessing the fine
options.c: A compliance program automatically guarantees full immunity from fines
options.d: Only state-certified compliance programs may be taken into account

kartellrecht-bussgelder-02.explanation: Sec. 81d GWB (introduced by the 10th GWB amendment, 2021) expressly names "appropriate and effective precautions to prevent and detect violations" as a circumstance to be considered in fine assessment - both precautions taken before the violation and clarification/cooperation efforts afterward. This is a mitigation, not a guarantee: if the violation was orchestrated by company management itself, the mitigation effectively does not apply.

kartellrecht-bussgelder-03.question: In August 2026 the Bundeskartellamt fined six road-construction companies EUR 60.3 million for years of customer allocation and bid-rigging. How, per the Bundeskartellamt, did the companies disguise their price coordination?

options.a: They exclusively used encrypted email software
options.b: They met only once a year at an official trade fair
options.c: They met monthly in Kassel and used coded terms such as mileage readings, beer, or sausage prices as stand-ins for bid figures
options.d: The coordination was conducted exclusively through an intermediary lawyer

kartellrecht-bussgelder-03.explanation: In this case, competitors met monthly during the construction season in Kassel and communicated coordination by phone, email, or messenger using coded terms (mileage readings, beer or sausage prices, sponsorship amounts, hotel room rates) as cover for actual bid figures - a textbook example of how cartel coordination is disguised in practice. Alongside the corporate fine under Sec. 1 GWB, individuals involved are under investigation for possible bid-rigging under Sec. 298 StGB.

kartellrecht-bussgelder-04.question: What is the Bundeskartellamt's stance on "checkbox compliance" (mechanically ticking off as many measures as possible)?

options.a: It requires exactly 9 mandatory measures from every undertaking regardless of size
options.b: It mandates a fixed annual training requirement for all employees
options.c: It explicitly rejects mechanically implementing as many measures as possible, instead requiring a program genuinely tailored - and effective - relative to the undertaking's size, organization, and risk
options.d: It leaves it entirely up to undertakings whether a compliance program makes sense at all

kartellrecht-bussgelder-04.explanation: The Bundeskartellamt explicitly stresses that effective compliance does not consist of mechanically implementing as many measures as possible. It names nine flexible, non-mandatory "building blocks" (including risk analysis, tone from the top, staff training/selection, whistleblower systems) - but does not prescribe any specific training frequency or fixed review interval. This differs markedly from the GwG, which imposes an explicit ongoing training duty for anti-money-laundering compliance.

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-01.question: What three requirements must an undertaking satisfy under Sec. 125(1) GWB to regain eligibility for public contracts despite a competition-law violation ("self-cleaning")?

options.a: Dismissal of management, payment of a state penalty, and dissolution of the affected department
options.b: Only full payment of the imposed fine
options.c: A public admission of guilt, an internal investigation, and an apology to competitors
options.d: Compensation for damage, comprehensive clarification of the facts through active cooperation, and concrete technical, organizational, and personnel measures to prevent future violations

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-01.explanation: Sec. 125(1) GWB cumulatively requires: (1) compensation for any damage caused by the offense, (2) comprehensive clarification of the facts and circumstances through active cooperation with the investigating authorities, and (3) concrete technical, organizational, and personnel measures suitable to prevent further violations. All three requirements must be satisfied together - none alone suffices.

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-02.question: Where exactly does improved employee competition-law training fit within self-cleaning under Sec. 125 GWB?

options.a: It is a standalone-sufficient requirement, independent of the other two requirements
options.b: It forms part of the "concrete technical, organizational, and personnel measures" (No. 3) - one of three requirements that must all be satisfied simultaneously, not sufficient on its own
options.c: It is not mentioned in the statute at all and is purely voluntary
options.d: It fully substitutes for the duty to compensate damage

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-02.explanation: Improved training is part of the technical, organizational, and personnel measures named in Sec. 125(1) No. 3 GWB - the statute names these three aspects together as one combined third requirement, not as separately labeled categories. It is not sufficient alone, however: compensation for damage (No. 1) and comprehensive fact clarification through cooperation (No. 2) must also be satisfied.

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-03.question: What must the contracting authority (or the Bundeskartellamt) do under Sec. 125(2) GWB if it considers the self-cleaning measures taken by the undertaking insufficient?

options.a: It may permanently exclude the undertaking from all tender procedures without further justification
options.b: It must give the undertaking the reasons for that decision
options.c: It must automatically initiate a new fine proceeding
options.d: It must submit the decision to a court for binding confirmation before it becomes effective

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-03.explanation: Sec. 125(2) GWB requires the contracting authority or the Bundeskartellamt to evaluate the measures taken, considering the severity and particular circumstances of the offense - if it considers them insufficient, it must give the undertaking the reasons for that decision - the statute does not prescribe a specific form (no explicit written-form requirement). This creates transparency and a basis for the undertaking to improve its measures or challenge the decision.

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-04.question: What does self-cleaning under Sec. 125 GWB practically achieve - what can it exempt an undertaking from?

options.a: Payment of an already legally binding fine
options.b: From an exclusion from public tender procedures that would otherwise apply because of the competition-law violation - mandatory under Sec. 123 GWB, or at the contracting authority's discretion under Sec. 124 GWB
options.c: The individual criminal liability of involved persons under Sec. 298 StGB
options.d: The obligation to notify future mergers to the Bundeskartellamt

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-04.explanation: Sec. 125 GWB concerns the public-procurement side: an undertaking that would otherwise have to be excluded from public tender procedures because of a competition-law violation can regain its eligibility through successful self-cleaning. To be precise: Sec. 123 GWB lists mandatory exclusion grounds, while Sec. 124 GWB lists facultative (discretionary, contracting-authority's-choice) exclusion grounds - pure competition-law administrative offenses typically fall under the discretionary exclusion ground in Sec. 124 GWB, so exclusion is not automatically mandatory in every case. The fine itself, and any individual criminal liability under Sec. 298 StGB, remain unaffected by self-cleaning.

kartellrecht-straftaten-01.question: What criminal consequence does an individual face under Sec. 298 StGB for submitting a tender offer based on an unlawful agreement?

options.a: Only a fine of at most EUR 1,000
options.b: Imprisonment of up to 5 years, or a fine
options.c: Mandatorily at least 2 years' imprisonment without suspension
options.d: No criminal consequences at all - only the involved undertakings can be held liable

kartellrecht-straftaten-01.explanation: Sec. 298 StGB (bid-rigging in public tenders) criminalizes submitting a tender offer based on an unlawful (cartel) agreement - imprisonment of up to 5 years, or a fine (Abs. 1). Abs. 2 extends this to negotiated-award procedures following a prior competitive process. This is individual criminal liability, in addition to the corporate fine under the GWB.

kartellrecht-straftaten-02.question: What possibility does Sec. 298(3) StGB provide for a person who was involved in a bid-rigging agreement but voluntarily reverses it?

options.a: No such possibility exists under the statute
options.b: Automatic exemption from punishment through mere subsequent regret, without further action
options.c: Exemption from punishment if the person voluntarily prevents the rigged offer's acceptance, or voluntarily and genuinely attempts to do so
options.d: Only a 50% reduction in sentence, never full exemption from punishment

kartellrecht-straftaten-02.explanation: Sec. 298(3) StGB contains a voluntary-withdrawal provision: a person who voluntarily prevents the rigged offer's acceptance, or genuinely and seriously attempts to do so, remains exempt from punishment. This requires active conduct - mere internal regret without action does not suffice.

kartellrecht-straftaten-03.question: Unlike money-laundering law (GwG), is there a statutorily fixed minimum frequency for competition-law compliance training?

options.a: Yes, at least once a year for all customer-facing employees
options.b: No - neither the GWB nor the Bundeskartellamt's administrative practice prescribes a specific training frequency; expectations scale to the undertaking's size, structure, and risk
options.c: Yes, every two years under a binding EU directive
options.d: No, training is entirely irrelevant in competition law and is never taken into account

kartellrecht-straftaten-03.explanation: Unlike Sec. 6(2) No. 6 GwG (which prescribes an explicit, ongoing training duty for anti-money-laundering compliance), competition law has no fixed, statutorily mandated training frequency. The Bundeskartellamt assesses the effectiveness of a compliance program - including training - case by case, based on the undertaking's size, structure, and risk profile, not on a rigid calendar interval.

kartellrecht-straftaten-04.question: In the road-construction cartel case, four of the involved companies received a reduction in their fine. Through which instrument is such a reduction typically achieved?

options.a: Through an out-of-court settlement directly with the harmed customers
options.b: Through the leniency program (Bonusregelung) - an undertaking that discloses its involvement in a cartel and actively cooperates with the authorities can receive a fine reduction or full immunity
options.c: By proving that competition was not actually affected in practice
options.d: By making a voluntary additional payment to the state treasury

kartellrecht-straftaten-04.explanation: The Bundeskartellamt's leniency program (Bonusregelung) rewards undertakings that are first to disclose their cartel involvement and cooperate comprehensively with a fine reduction, up to and including full immunity. In the road-construction case, four companies obtained a reduction this way - a strong incentive to self-report violations early rather than conceal them.

kartellrecht-grundlagen-05.question: Sec. 18 GWB defines when an undertaking is dominant. What does Sec. 19 GWB prohibit such an undertaking from doing - and what, notably, does it not prohibit?

options.a: Sec. 19 GWB already prohibits holding a dominant position as such
options.b: Sec. 19 GWB prohibits dominant undertakings from any price increase without Bundeskartellamt approval
options.c: Only the abuse of the position is prohibited (Sec. 19(1) GWB) - subsection 2 lists examples such as unfairly impeding or, without objective justification, treating other undertakings differently (exclusionary abuse) and demanding prices or terms deviating from those that would result under effective competition (exploitative abuse); the dominant position itself remains lawful
options.d: Sec. 19 GWB is directed exclusively at cartel agreements between multiple dominant undertakings

kartellrecht-grundlagen-05.explanation: Sec. 19(1) GWB prohibits the abuse of a dominant position, not the position itself - market leadership earned through superior performance is lawful. Sec. 19(2) GWB lists standard examples: No. 1 covers exclusionary abuse (unfairly impeding or discriminating against other undertakings), No. 2 exploitative abuse (prices or terms deviating from those that would very likely result under effective competition), No. 4 includes refusing access to data, networks, or infrastructure facilities for adequate remuneration, and No. 5 the so-called "tapping" prohibition (demanding advantages without objective justification). The provision mirrors Art. 102 TFEU and targets unilateral conduct - unlike Sec. 1 GWB, no agreement between multiple undertakings is required.

kartellrecht-grundlagen-06.question: A manufacturer contractually dictates to its dealers the exact retail price at which they must resell its products. Is this permissible because manufacturer and dealer are not competitors?

options.a: Yes - the cartel prohibition applies only to horizontal agreements between competitors
options.b: No - resale price maintenance (imposing fixed or minimum resale prices) is a hardcore restriction under Sec. 1 GWB / Art. 101 TFEU even as a vertical agreement; only non-binding recommended prices and maximum prices without pressure or incentives are permitted
options.c: Yes, as long as the imposed price is in line with the market
options.d: No, but only if the manufacturer is also dominant under Sec. 18 GWB

kartellrecht-grundlagen-06.explanation: Sec. 1 GWB and Art. 101 TFEU cover not only horizontal agreements between competitors but also vertical agreements between different market levels (e.g. manufacturer and dealer). Resale price maintenance - imposing fixed resale prices or minimum resale prices - is expressly a hardcore restriction under Art. 4(a) of the Vertical Block Exemption Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2022/720), removing the agreement's exemption: it deprives the dealer of pricing freedom as a central parameter of competition. Maximum prices and non-binding recommended retail prices remain permissible - but only as long as they do not effectively operate as fixed or minimum prices through pressure (e.g. threats to cut off supply) or incentives.

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-05.question: The Bundeskartellamt or the EU Commission arrives unannounced to search your business premises (a "dawn raid"). What is the correct way for the company to respond?

options.a: Employees may quickly delete incriminating documents as long as the inspectors have not yet entered the room
options.b: The company may refuse entry until its own lawyer arrives - the authority must wait as long as necessary
options.c: Submit to the inspection and cooperate: inspectors may enter premises, examine and copy records, and seal premises and records; counsel may be called in, but obstruction - such as breaking a seal or deleting data - is punished with separate fines of its own
options.d: Only EU Commission inspections must be tolerated - the Bundeskartellamt always needs management's consent

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-05.explanation: Under Sec. 59b GWB the competition authority may search business premises - in principle with a judicial warrant from the local court, and in exigent circumstances (Gefahr im Verzug) exceptionally without one. The EU Commission has corresponding inspection powers under Art. 20 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2003: entering premises, examining and copying business records, sealing premises and records, and requesting explanations. Counsel may be called in, but inspectors are not required to wait indefinitely for their arrival. Obstruction is expensive: under Art. 23(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2003 it carries fines of up to 1 percent of total turnover - in 2008 the Commission fined E.ON EUR 38 million for a single broken seal, upheld by the EU courts. Practical rule: cooperate, destroy nothing, open nothing that has been sealed, and immediately inform the legal department and external counsel.

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-06.question: When must a merger be notified to the European Commission - and how does merger control differ from the cartel prohibition?

options.a: Every acquisition of an EU-based company must be notified, regardless of turnover
options.b: Once the EUMR turnover thresholds are met - in the primary case a combined worldwide turnover of all parties above EUR 5 billion and an EU-wide turnover of at least EUR 250 million for each of at least two parties - prior notification is mandatory and the transaction may not be implemented until cleared (standstill obligation); merger control reviews planned concentrations in advance, whereas the cartel prohibition sanctions prohibited coordination between undertakings that remain independent
options.c: Notification is always voluntary - the Commission can only prohibit mergers after the fact
options.d: Mergers are a sub-category of the cartel prohibition under Art. 101 TFEU and are fined under the same rules

kartellrecht-kernbeschraenkungen-06.explanation: The EU Merger Regulation (Regulation (EC) No 139/2004, EUMR) is a standalone preventive regime alongside the cartel prohibition: concentrations with a Union dimension must be notified before implementation under Art. 4(1) EUMR and may only be implemented after clearance under Art. 7(1) EUMR. A Union dimension exists in the primary case under Art. 1(2) EUMR where the parties' combined worldwide turnover exceeds EUR 5 billion and at least two parties each have an EU-wide turnover above EUR 250 million (exception: the two-thirds rule, where each party achieves more than two-thirds of its EU turnover in one and the same Member State; Art. 1(3) contains alternative, lower thresholds). Breaching the notification duty or the standstill obligation ("gun jumping") can be fined with up to 10 percent of total turnover under Art. 14 EUMR. The difference from the cartel prohibition: merger control reviews a lasting structural change in advance, while the cartel prohibition sanctions coordination between undertakings that remain legally independent.

kartellrecht-bussgelder-05.question: An internationally active sales employee claims: "Cartel violations are just a matter of corporate fines everywhere." Why is this a dangerous misconception for a multinational group?

options.a: Because in Germany, too, every cartel agreement automatically results in imprisonment for those involved
options.b: Because fines can only be imposed on individuals, never on companies
options.c: Because individual criminal exposure differs sharply between jurisdictions: in Germany, cartel violations are administrative offenses (Ordnungswidrigkeiten) for companies, and only bid-rigging is individually criminal under Sec. 298 StGB - whereas in the US, individuals face up to 10 years' imprisonment and a USD 1 million fine for price-fixing, market-allocation, and bid-rigging conspiracies, and in the UK the "cartel offence" carries up to 5 years' imprisonment
options.d: Because cartel violations are generally not prosecuted outside Germany

kartellrecht-bussgelder-05.explanation: Germany treats cartel violations by companies as administrative offenses (fines under Sec. 81 ff. GWB); there is no general individual cartel crime - only bid-rigging in tenders is individually criminal under Sec. 298 StGB. Other jurisdictions go considerably further: in the US, a violation of Sec. 1 of the Sherman Act is a felony - individuals face up to 10 years' imprisonment and fines of up to USD 1 million (corporations up to USD 100 million, in each case increasable to twice the gain or loss), and the Department of Justice actively prosecutes managers. In the United Kingdom, the "cartel offence" under s. 188 Enterprise Act 2002 criminalizes individual participation in price-fixing, market-sharing, output-limitation, and bid-rigging arrangements - up to 5 years' imprisonment (s. 190). For employees with international business, personal criminal liability is therefore real - not merely a corporate risk.

kartellrecht-bussgelder-06.question: The authority's fine often does not end a cartel case for the company. What applies to private damages actions by cartel victims under Secs. 33a ff. GWB?

options.a: Only state bodies can claim damages, not private customers
options.b: Injured parties (e.g. customers) can claim damages; it is rebuttably presumed that a cartel causes damage (Sec. 33a(2) GWB), and the competition authority's final infringement finding binds the civil court (Sec. 33b GWB) - so "follow-on" claimants do not have to prove the violation again
options.c: Damages actions are barred once the company has paid the fine in full
options.d: The civil court must re-investigate the cartel violation from scratch in every damages case - authority decisions have no effect whatsoever

kartellrecht-bussgelder-06.explanation: Sec. 33a(1) GWB imposes liability for damage caused by an intentional or negligent competition-law violation; Sec. 33a(2) GWB contains the rebuttable presumption that a cartel causes damage - so the claimant does not have to prove the occurrence of harm from scratch. Under Sec. 33b GWB, the civil court is bound by the final infringement finding of the competition authority, the EU Commission, or a competition authority of another EU Member State - the practical foundation of the follow-on action. Sec. 33e GWB contains an important exception: a leniency applicant granted full immunity from the fine is in principle liable only to its own direct and indirect customers and suppliers - to other injured parties only insofar as they cannot obtain full compensation from the remaining cartel members. Cartel damages can substantially exceed the fine itself, making them a compliance argument in their own right.

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-05.question: A company has been entered into the competition register (Wettbewerbsregister) at the Bundeskartellamt because of a cartel fine. How long does the entry remain - and how can the company get it removed early?

options.a: Entries remain permanently and can never be deleted
options.b: Entries are deleted after 10 years; early deletion is not provided for by law
options.c: Fine decisions are deleted at the latest 3 years after they are issued, entries based on certain criminal convictions at the latest after 5 years (Sec. 7 WRegG); early deletion is available on application to the register authority if the company demonstrates successful self-cleaning (Sec. 8 WRegG)
options.d: Deletion happens automatically as soon as the fine is paid

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-05.explanation: The Competition Register Act (WRegG) governs the nationwide register at the Bundeskartellamt, which contracting authorities must consult before awarding public contracts. Sec. 7 WRegG staggers the deletion periods: entries based on fine decisions (which include cartel fines) are deleted at the latest 3 years after the fine decision is issued; entries based on certain criminal convictions at the latest 5 years after the decision becomes final. Before the period expires, Sec. 8 WRegG offers a route out: the company can apply to the register authority for early deletion based on self-cleaning and must demonstrate its self-cleaning measures - for procurement-law exclusion grounds, measured against the standard of Sec. 125 GWB (compensation for damage, active clarification cooperation, concrete preventive measures). The application is subject to fees. Once the entry is deleted, the underlying facts may no longer be held against the company in tender procedures.

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-06.question: How does self-cleaning under Sec. 125 GWB relate to EU law?

options.a: Self-cleaning is a purely German invention with no European basis
options.b: Sec. 125 GWB implements Art. 57(6) of the EU Public Procurement Directive 2014/24/EU - the Directive guarantees undertakings across the Union the right to demonstrate their reliability through compensation for damage, active clarification cooperation, and concrete preventive measures, and additionally caps the maximum exclusion period (5 years for mandatory, 3 years for facultative exclusion grounds)
options.c: EU law prohibits self-cleaning - Sec. 125 GWB therefore applies only to purely national tenders
options.d: The EU Directive governs only fines; there is no EU law on procurement debarment

kartellrecht-selbstreinigung-06.explanation: Art. 57(6) of Directive 2014/24/EU is the EU-law foundation of self-cleaning: an economic operator affected by an exclusion ground may prove that it has paid or undertaken to pay compensation for damage caused, has comprehensively clarified the facts and circumstances by actively collaborating with the investigating authorities, and has taken concrete technical, organisational, and personnel measures appropriate to prevent further misconduct - exactly the three requirements Sec. 125(1) GWB transposes into German law. The duty to give reasons when measures are deemed insufficient (Sec. 125(2) GWB) also stems from the Directive. Art. 57(7) additionally caps the maximum exclusion period: at most 5 years for mandatory and at most 3 years for facultative exclusion grounds - implemented in Germany in Sec. 126 GWB. For internationally active companies this means the self-cleaning logic applies EU-wide in every Member State, not only in Germany.

kartellrecht-straftaten-05.question: A company discloses its involvement in bid-rigging through the leniency program and receives full immunity from the corporate fine. Does this also protect the employees involved from criminal prosecution under Sec. 298 StGB?

options.a: Yes - the company's leniency status automatically extends to all employees
options.b: No - the leniency program of Secs. 81h ff. GWB concerns only the remission or reduction of fines in cartel administrative-offense proceedings; prosecution under Sec. 298 StGB is a matter for the public prosecutor's office, and German law contains no formal, automatic immunity guarantee for the individuals involved
options.c: Yes, but only for management-level employees
options.d: No, because the leniency program categorically excludes any fine reduction in bid-rigging cases

kartellrecht-straftaten-05.explanation: Secs. 81h ff. GWB codify the leniency program exclusively for cartel fine proceedings: cooperation is rewarded with remission or reduction of the fine - an administrative-offense sanction. Criminal prosecution for bid-rigging (Sec. 298 StGB), by contrast, lies with the public prosecutor's office, which is bound by the principle of mandatory prosecution; the Bundeskartellamt cannot dispose of it. Unlike, for example, the US leniency program, which promises the first applicant non-prosecution of its cooperating employees as well, German law has no formal individual immunity guarantee attached to the company's leniency status. An individual's cooperation may mitigate the sentence or lead to a discontinuation - but that is not a guarantee. For compliance officers this means: the company's leniency decision and the defense interests of the individual employees involved must be assessed and advised on separately.

kartellrecht-straftaten-06.question: A company internally discovers indications of cartel involvement but has not yet fully worked through the facts. Why can the so-called marker under Sec. 81m GWB be decisive in this situation?

options.a: The marker obliges the authority to suspend proceedings for at least one year
options.b: The marker fully replaces the later leniency application - no further submissions are needed
options.c: With the marker, the company initially only declares its willingness to cooperate, using a few minimum details, and thereby secures its rank in the order of leniency applications; if it files the fully worked-out application within the deadline set, the marker's timestamp counts - decisive, because as a rule only the first applicant can obtain full immunity from the fine, while later applicants get only a reduction
options.d: The marker automatically shields all involved employees from criminal prosecution

kartellrecht-straftaten-06.explanation: Sec. 81m GWB codifies the marker system: a cartel participant can approach the competition authority to initially declare only its willingness to cooperate and thereby obtain a rank in the order of receipt of leniency applications. The marker must contain minimum details - including name and address, the other cartel participants, the products and territories affected, the duration and nature of the conduct, and information on leniency applications filed with other authorities. The authority then sets a reasonable deadline for the fully worked-out application; if it is met, the marker's timestamp determines the application's rank. This matters enormously in practice because the leniency program is a race: full immunity is as a rule reserved for the first applicant, and all later applicants can only obtain a reduction. A company that wants to "finish clarifying everything internally" before contacting the authority risks another cartel member getting there first - and taking the immunity with them.
